newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban victory restores militia's morale.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban victory restores militia's morale.

text.p: The success of Taleban forces on the front line north of Afghanistan's capital Kabul has broken a six-week deadlock in the battle and restored the militia's morale, analysts said on Sunday.

On Friday and Saturday, the fundamentalist Islamic Taleban, who took Kabul in late September, managed to push back the forces of the opposition alliance more than 10 km (six miles) to a position where the Taleban now threaten Bagram airbase and the mouth of the Panjsher valley.
The valley is the main base of operations for opposition military commander Ahmed Shah Masood.

In a bloody 24-hour engagement, the Taleban said they killed dozens of opposition fighters and captured tanks and artillery. The Taleban also said they had taken more than 200 prisoners, a huge number in the context of the limited engagements that have characterised much of the fighting in Afghanistan to date.

The Taleban front line commander in the area told journalists the attack was just the first step in their plan to destroy the opposition and take the stronghold of opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, the town of Mazar-i-Sharif, in the north of the country close to the border of the former Soviet Union.

"Our operation against the pagan Dostum will continue as soon as the civilians evacuate the area. We will go on until his forces are completely annihilated from here to Mazar-i-Sharif," Maulawi Jalaluddin Haqqani, the Taleban's senior commander in the area, told journalists on Saturday.
A pathetic procession of hundreds of men, women and children were fleeing the war zone on foot and in trucks. Haqqani said the Taleban had provided some transport.
On Saturday, the opposition retaliated to the Taleban advance with four air raids on Kabul itself and a number of others against Taleban front line positions.
Hospitals in Kabul reported six civilian casualties from the raids, and one woman injured in the head from falling anti-aircraft rounds.

The raids were centred on Kabul's airport, which is used for both military and civilian traffic, and the Presidential Palace in the centre of the city. The palace is off limits and it was not possible to ascertain if there were any casualties there.
There were reports of minor damage to the airport, but U.N. workers, who use it to ferry supplies and personnel into Kabul, said on Sunday they intended to continue using it.

The territory that the Taleban captured in their advance puts them within five km (three miles) of Bagram airbase. However the base has been under the guns of the Taleban for more than a month, limiting its strategic value to the opposition.
Afghan watchers say that the air raids on Kabul were launched from northern bases controlled by Dostum.

More significant is the loss to the opposition of the village of Istalif, which lies on a spur of the Hindu Kush mountain range. The village provides an elevated firebase from which the Taleban can harass their forces in the broad valley which cradles the battle-front.
Perhaps the biggest blow to the opposition forces will be to their morale. They have launched a number of offensives against the Taleban in the past weeks, but have been unable to dislodge them.
One Afghan watcher said he believed that the defeat would further weaken the bonds between the members of the opposition alliance.

"The opposition alliance was a marriage of necessity in the face of the Taleban victory in Kabul. The members of the alliance fought each other to a standstill in Kabul in 1994 and there is still a lot of mistrust there," said the observer, who wished to remain anonymous.
"Many of the people who were killed and captured (in the recent offensive) were Dostum's men, and I can't see that improving morale, or trust, between the allies."
